On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In view of the promise I made last evening, I should like to make a statement with respect to the depositors of the Home Bank:
On July 17, 1924, this House unanimously adopted the report of the committee on Banking and Commerce with respect to the losses sustained by the depositors of the Home Bank of Canada. The concluding paragraph of the said report is as follows:
Your committee consider that the facts brought out in the interim report submitted by Mr. Chief Justice McKeown, and the evidence therein referred to, establish that the depositors of the Home Bank have a moral claim in equity for compensation by the country on account of any loss they may suffer by reason of the failure of the Home Bank.
In the circumstances, the government has decided to introduce, this session, a measure recognizing, with respect to the depositors of the Home Bank, "the moral claim in equity for compensation", as referred to in this paragraph of the report. The proposed legislation will be brought down in due course.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I wish to make an observ-

Supply-Post Office
ation with reference to the first sentence of the Prime Minister's statement, and I make it without regard at all to what the attitude of the opposition may be towards the measure. The reference was to the "unanimous" adoption of a report. There were many reports adopted in this way hastily last session against my vigorous protest, and I stated at the time on more than one occasion that I did not consider such adoption as in any way binding the House to the terms of the report. That is the position I take still. In this connection I want to ask whether the amount which the government proposes to give is to be in the supplementary estimates, and also why it is not in the main estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The bill which will be introduced will indicate the amount; there is no reason why the estimate should be given before the bill is presented.
Will the amount be in the supplementary estimates if the bill passes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It will depend on the action the House takes with reference to the bill.
But if the bill passes, will the amount be in the supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The House will be asked to vote whatever amount is required, and I presume the request will be made in the usual order.

That does not answer the question. The question is whether it will be put in the supplementary estimates or not. Whether the government does it in the usual order or whether it does not, will the amount be provided in the supplementary estimates, assuming that the bill will pass?

The House in committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Civil Government-Post Office-Salaries, including amount required to pay allowance to office appliance operators, grade 2 operating Hollerith card punching machines, in accordance with provisions of Order in Council P.C. 156/2521 dated December 24, 1923, $1,143,729. Contingencies, $195,000.

Mr. Chairman, the committee will
observe that the salary items in this estimate refer only to salaries paid at Ottawa in the inside service; they have no reference to anything in the outside service. There is but little substantial difference between the amount of the estimate this year and that of last year. It will be noticed that last year the House voted $1,109,518 for these services, while this year the committee is asked to vote $1,143,729, or an increase of a little over $34,000. That increase is made up of statutory increases to the extent of about $28,000, and the balance is represented by amounts required on account of salary revision by the Civil Service Commission and the reorganization effected in the department through the same body. The number of employees, it will be observed, has increased by 25. Twenty of these new positions are what are known as office appliance operators, and are due to the introduction of what is known as the Hollerith system for mechanical sor'tation and audit of money orders and postal notes. In this connection it will be noticed that last year the amount for contingencies was $145,000, this year it is $195,000, or a difference of about $50,000. Now this difference is accounted for wholly by the introduction of the system to which I have just referred. The $50,000 is made up of two items:	One for the purchase of 23,000,000
cards used in connection with the system of mechanical sortation and audit, and the other for the rental paid for the machines which perform the work. It may be stated for the information of the committee that if this system had not been introduced the department would have had to provide for the salaries of about 100 additional employees to carry on the work as it was carried on under the old method. In times past it frequently happened that this work was in arrear, sometimes to the extent of two years, but under this new system the work is kept up to date;

Supply-Post Office

and whereas in former times, from 140 to 150 employees sorted and audited about 32,000 money order cards per day, under the new system 113 employees can handle over 50,000 orders a day and make out about 50,000 cards per day. This system has perfected the work in one branch of an important public service, and the officials who are in charge of it under the Financial Superintendent would be glad if members of the House would drop into the Union Bank building, where it is installed, and see the system in operation.
The estimates last year I see amounted to $1,109,518. What was actually spent?

I am informed that on
account of salaries there was expended for 1923-4 $1,034,603, and for contingencies $154,108.66.
How did the government manage to get the money when it was not voted?
We did not-it was carried over as a charge against the present year.

When machines are introduced in the course of ordinary business the usual effect is to reduce rather than t >
increase the number of employees. Will the minister explain the purpose of these machines? Perhaps some of us will have to go down and see them in order to understand them properly.
Are there any in use in other countries?
They are used at Washington. Officials from here went down and observed them in operation and made a report on them before their installation was decided upon.
Are they what is known as the International business machine, or of a similar type?
I have not heard that term applied to them. They are known as the Hollerith system for mechanical sortation and audit.
These machines are rented, not bought outright?
Yes, rented.
What is the rental for each machine?

There are different rentals for different classes of machines. Some rent at $8.50 a month, some at $30 a month, others, such -as the key-punching machines and the tabulators, rent at $57.50 and $75 a month.
Where are they made?
In the United States.

Notwithstanding the fact
that men have been laid off because of the introduction of these machines the total number of employees in -the department has increased by twenty-five. While 821 employees are provided for in the inside service this year, there were only 796 last year. The minister said these machines would do away with some forty or fifty employees.

There were posit'ons abolished during the year and there were other employees who went out at that time and were replaced by others on the staff. My statement was that if the old method had been pursued, owing to the increased volume of business there would have been an increase in the number of employees, but -because of the introduction of this system the number has been kept down. When employees having a maximum salary go out they are usually replaced by others in the service at the time who come in at the minimum salary. The increase in the amount that we are asking for is but slight

Supply-Post Office
compared with the number of employees who have been added. That is one of the reasons. Those who were displaced1 by reason of the introduction of the machines were absorbed into other branches of the department. That was one of the conditions on which the system was introduced-that there should not be any large reduction in the amount of labour employed.

I was not thinking especially of the increase in the amount of money spent, but rather of the increase in the number of employees. Even if an employee who has attained his maximum is replaced by another at a lower salary, it takes only one man to replace him. What I want to know is why there are 25 more employees in the inside service than there were the previous year, in spite of the changes due to the machines.
Perhaps I did not make that clear. It is due-not altogether-to the increase in business in this particular branch. There has been an increase of 25, I am informed, in the number of employees.

The conversation
may be very edifying, but we in this part of the chamber have not the faintest idea of what is going on at the upper end of it.
Are these machines purchased from an American concern direct, or through a Canadian agency?
They are rented through a Canadian agency, I am informed.
Who represents the Canadian agency?
They are represented in Canada, I understand, by a gentleman named Foran-not the gentleman who is secretary of the Civil Service Commission.
That of course, would be very surprising.

I am not quite clear
whether these machines are simply for tabulating records or whether they are used in the handling of mail.
They are for use in auditing money orders and postal notes.
Did the Customs department not try these machines and discard them?
Not that I ever heard of.
Partly.

It will be observed that in the number of office appliance operators there is an increase of twenty, and in the whole department an increase of twenty-five. I have been informed that the Customs department tested these machines over a period of years, in work similar to that for which the Post Office Department is using them, and found them unsuited to government work. If that is true, and in view of the increased cost and the increase in the number of employees, this seems to be a questionable innovation, particularly if there is no saving.

I have never said the Customs department tried these machines for any length of time, but even if they did and the machines were found unsuitable for the work in the Customs department, of course, it would not follow that they would be unsuitable in any other department. As a matter of fact, they suit this particular work admirably, and as I have pointed out if it were not for the introduction of these machines we would have to engage at least one hundred additional employees to cope with the greater volume of work.
What is the revenue expected this year from the department, and how does it compare with last year?
I have not that statement on hand, but I will be glad to get it for my right hon. friend on another item, and we can discuss it then.
I think the minister has a pretty good idea; nobody would have any better.
At the moment I am sorry I have not.

I have no information I would want to become authority for, but I understand the revenue is less. Now, with a smaller revenue, we have a larger personnel, and all these Hollerith machines. How does the minister account for so much more money being required when the revenue received is so much less?

I have explained the reason for the additional amount required. As to the revenue, I have not a statement on hand, but I shall be very glad to get it and let my right hon. friend have it. As a matter of fact, the officials upon whom of course I have to rely for all this information, assure me that the expenditure would be very, very much greater were it not for the introduction of this system; that money has been saved
Supply-Post Office

by its introduction; speed has been attained in the doing of the work; and, of equal importance, greater accuracy has been obtained.
It looks pretty bad if only for these precious machines we would have one hundred and1 twenty-five more employees than last year.
Provided the volume of work kept up.
Why is there such a volume of work? The post office is not increasing its functions that I know of, and it is not increasing its revenue. Why is the work increasing at head office?
The money order business has increased twenty-five per cent. It has been one of the most remarkable increases in connection with the department.
Does the head office here have much to do with the general money order business?

Yes, in connection with auditing. After these money orders have been paid and certified, they are sent in here to the Pinancial branch of the department, and it is there that this audit work is done, and there that the arrears of work I have spoken of have accumulated.
I suppose money is going out to pay for foreign manufactures. Where is the money all going?

My hon. friend knows that a man may go into the post office in Ottawa, for instance, and get a money order payable on an office in Winnipeg. The Winnipeg office deals with the payee, and when the transaction is completed as between the Post Office Department and the member of the public entitled to receive payment, these orders, and a list certified by the official in charge in the paying office, are sent to Ottawa, where the audit takes place in the Financial branch of the department.

I see there has been some change in the number of audit clerks employed. The number of senior audit clerks has been reduced from 16 to 15; one has been let out there. Then in audit clerks there is an increase from 2 to 5, an increase of three; so there has been a net increase in those two staffs of two. Then there is an increase in senior clerks of two, making the net increase four. There is also an increase in clerk-bookkeepers of one, making the net increase five; also an increase in account

clerks of two, making the net increase seven. The only other increase that I notice is in the office of appliance operators, where the increase is from 61 to 81. There is one other decrease which would make the net increase in the inside staff of the Post Office Department twenty-five. That would hardly account for the large increase now asked for by the minister. Last year under this item we voted $1,109,518; this year we are asked to vote $1,143,729, an increase roughly of about $34,000. Do I understand that the whole of that $34,000 is required to pay the extra salaries of the twenty-five new assistants taken on in the department?
Perhaps my hon. friend was not in when I explained that of the $34,000 increase, about $28,000 in round numbers, represented statutory increases over which, of course, the department has no control.
When is it likely that statutory increases will cease?
Never.

Then will there always be more expenditure for all time to come on account of statutory increases? It seems to me that when there are employees coming in at the bottom there will be some going out at the top, and that the time should come when there would be no increase, that there would be a balance struck. But for a number of years, ever since I came into this House, the vote on account of statutory increases grows. Will that always go on?

There is a minimum and maximum salary for each class. An employee begins at the minimum and receives automatically an increase each year until he reaches the maximum for his class, when the statutory increases for him stop. These are matters fixed by the Civil Service Commission, under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. But each year as my hon. friend has mentioned, there are people coming in at the minimum salaries, and therefore statutory increases have to be provided for them.

When one new employee
comes in at the minimum salary, does it not happen that one goes out at the top who is drawing the maximum salary? Or, is the staff to increase for all time to come?

No, the staff increases
only in proportion as the work increases, only as there are increased duties to be performed.' There are changes, of course, in the different branches of the department, and in the net result there has been an increase this year, as I have already explained.

Supply-Post Office
That same net result seems to happen every year.
No.

I would have no objection personally to these statutory increases. I think the officials are paid little enough, and in many cases they are paid too little. I understood the minister to say that of the increased vote asked for this year-$34,000 in round numbers-$28,000 was to be applied to statutory increases under the act. That would leave only $6,000 to be spent on the twenty-five new employees, or an average of $240 for each employee. Surely there must be some discrepancy there. I doubt if such a sum as $28,000 is necessary for the statutory increases. Would the minister explain that?

Perhaps I had better give the details as furnished by the department. My statement as to $28,000 in round numbers being required for statutory increases is substantially correct. There were 379 statu-ory increases, amounting to $27,900 New positions 28 in number called for an amount aggregate of $25,260. There are: Two senior clerks at $1,320; one clerk bookkeeper at $1,020; three audit clerks $960; two account clerks $960; twenty office appliance operators, grade 2, $840. Then there is an increase due to salary revision by the Civil Service Commission, $3,180, and increases due to re-organization by the same body, $1,180. Adding all these increases together we have a total of $57,520. Now, set off against that, are the following decreases:	Three positions not required owing to re-organization $5,080, the difference between salaries of employees who have been promoted or who have left the service and salaries of persons promoted or appomted to replace them at lower salaries, $18,229; or a total decrease of $23,309. Deducting the total decrease from the total increases there is a net increase of $34,211. That is how the amount is made up.
Would the minister give a statement showing the volume of the money order business done over a period of three years and the cost to the department of doing that business for those years?
Those are the charges?'
No, those are the receipts from the money order business. Does my right hon. friend mean by "charges" the expenditure for salaries and so on?
No I mean the commissions on the orders.

There is a material decrease in the last fiscal year as compared with
1921-	2.

There is an increase over
1922-	3, but a decrease as compared with 1921-2.
Just where did the increases in the volume of business come in?

Perhaps my hon. friend misunderstood me on that point. I was not speaking of the amount, but the increase in the number of orders handled. The increase was, roughly, a little over two and a half millions.
Would the minister tell us whether he has made a definite term contract for the use of these machines, and if so for how long?

My information is that there is not a definite term contract. The machines are rented for an indefinite time and as long as they suit. They may be rejected or exchanged whenever the department sees fit.
Will the minister explain why the profits of the department have decreased very materially whereas the volume of business appears to have increased?

The explanation, I am informed, is that there is just the same amount of work required in handling a money order for a small amount as for a large amount,, and that the number of orders for small amounts has increased in number over those of larger amounts.
How many machines have been installed and what is the total monthly or annual rental?

Perhaps before the
minister answers he will permit a word of comment on his last explanation. The explanation was that the number of small orders had increased out of proportion to the number
Supply-Post Office

of orders for large sums-that the amount of work on a small order was just as much as on a large order. That is the reason why- although there was a larger business, a larger number of orders, and a larger total-the profits now are less than they were three years ago. Does not the minister see that it follows from his explanation that the small order business is done at a loss?.
In reply to my right hon. friend I would say wre would lose a great deal more if the other system were in vogue.
What other system?

As indicated by a question a short time ago the amount is determined by the commissions paid. There is the variance that was mentioned, there is no doubt about that. In reply to my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) who inquired as to the number of machines in use-

And the monthly or annual
rental paid.

-I may say there are 30 key punch machines at $8.50 a month; 13 sorting machines at $30 a month; 7 tabulators at $57.50 a month; and 1 tabulator at $75 a month. Then besides, in the postal note division, there are 12 key punch machines at $8.50 a month; 4 sorting machines at $30 a month; and 3 tabulators at $75 a month.
What is the total amount for the two departments?
The total is $18,834.

I am not very much
impressed with the minister's comment on my argument. I tried to show him that if he gave a right account to the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) of the reason for the loss of profits notwithstanding the increase in business-* it must mean that he is losing money on his small orders. When I pointed out that, his answer was that if we had done it the other way we would have lost more. I do not know what the "other way" is, but I would advise him not to get into a worse way. Surely the country is not going to understand that on the small order business of the Dominion it is losing money.
No.
That must be the case, or the answer the minister gave to the hon. member for Burrard is wrong.

I think my answer was correct.
cMr. Meighen.]

Could the hon. gentleman not speak as to a particular year? A certain year, let us say, thirty per cent of th? business is small order business and seventy ,per cent large order business. That year the profits are so much. Now in a later year there is forty per cent of the smaller business and sixty per cent of the larger business, but there is far more business and the profits are leas than they were previously. Now, to account for a less profit it must be that the small order business loses money. If it all makes money, then the more business there is the more money is made, in ail classes. But there is less money made. Therefore it cannot all make money. Why is it we are doing a great class of our business at a loss?
There may be less money made, but that does not of necessity entail a loss. It is the difference in one year compared to another.
If there is less money made because of an increase in a certain character of business, it must be because that certain character of business is a losing venture.

No. I will point out now something which I overlooked before, that there was a change in the rate of exchange which made a difference. A higher rate of exchange had to be paid to the United States than previously.

Would it not reduce the expenditure if the business of sending money through the post office were encouraged and the public were offered the opportunity to keep deposits in the post office savings banks, cheque out the money and have the cheques marked good in the office where the money was deposited? The big department stores keep deposit accounts for their customers and money is chequed out in that way. There is no great bookkeeping required and the system is very simple. I think we have a system in connection with the postal notes and money orders which is 4 p.m. altogether too elaborate. This method could be simplified by allowing the public to keep deposits at the post office, to issue cheques for any amounts they desire to withdraw, and to have the cheque marked good, as is done in the banks.

My hon. friend has touched upon a point that he and I have discussed more than once. A change has been made by allowing depositors to withdraw up to the sum of $25 without going through the for-

Supply-Post Office
maility of notice. The extension of that system has been under consideration, but it has to be borne in mind that what my hon. friend has in mind is rather a savings bank branch of the Post Office Department. Properly speaking it is not a part of the Post Office Department; it is in point of fact more properly a branch of the Department of Finance. Originally it was attached to the Post Office Department for the convenience of the public. The banking business is no part of the postal service. The post office savings bank, as I understand it, was designed to encourage people to deposit their savings and keep them there. A man may deposit money in the ordinary savings bank branch, but will proceed immediately to issue cheques. The two purposes are at their root different. But the suggestion of my hon. friend is well worth considering, and I will bring it to the attention of the superintendent.

I desire to draw the minister's attention to the fact that in the statement he gave to the House a few minutes ago he said that in the total number of money orders issued there had been an increase of 25 per cent. Now in addition -there has been an increase in the total amount of money orders of about twenty-three per cent, and yet there has been a decrease of approximately thirty per cent in commissions or profits earned by the department. That is something I cannot understand.

There is an increase as between last year and the year before. My idea is that the amount would be approximately as great were it not for the exchange which has to be paid on business with the United States.
Has the department considered purchasing the machines that have been mentioned?
No, the company owning them will not sell them.

The hon. minister says they will not sell the machines in this country. I say then that they should not be allowed to dictate the terms. When a company or anybody comes to this country and obtains a patent and is protected by that patent, if the government require the use of that machine, the government should compel them to deliver it to us.

Perhaps I should have
added in my explanation that an important part of the arrangement-and I have no doubt my hon. friend and the leading business men
of the country know it-is that the company undertakes to keep the machine in working order, so that no time is lost. That is a very important point.

Typewriter companies
adopt the same method, but they sell the machines.
The companies do it for no other reason than that it is a matter of great importance to them in the way of profits.
And it savours of monopoly.
Could the minister tell us the total revenue derived from the sale of these postal notes to the public?
For the last year it was $1,364,110.53.
Is that less than what is paid to the postmasters for preparing the notes?
I did not grasp the question.

The postmaster receives a
certain amount for issuing the notes, and I am asking if that amount is the total revenue.
No, that does not include the item mentioned by my hon. friend. That is just the total amount of commission.

I have been thinking
over the explanation the hon. minister gave for having voted last year $145,000 on contingencies and spending a lot more. His explanation was that there was still more to be voted. They anticipated the vote this year. Did they do it by Governor General's warrant?
No.
Out of what account did the money which was spent come?
The amount was not raised, but was charged against the amount which is asked for this year.

You have to have cash to pay cash. Where did the actual cash come from? There was no cash there. You might charge it against this year if this year's money was voted, but where did that money come from? It must have been a case of misappropriation if there was no money voted for it.

The only explanation I have is the one given me which I have transmitted to the hon. member. If there is any other I shall be glad to get it.
Supply-Post Office

Some money has been voted against which these cheques were issued. There must have been. It is a pretty free and easy way just to vote the money out of "any old" account and say: "Oh well, it will be voted next year in parliament". By the way, I noticed this morning in one of those press announcements with which the government always precedes an official statement of disaster the fact that this year's estimate is going to be made a lot less than last year's, by the very ingenious device of increasing last year's. Is this to be an instance?

My right hon. friend
must refer to some other department.

I suppose the same may apply to a few others as well. This explanation was very amusing and I hope it struck other hon. members the same way. I cannot help admiring the courage of a government that foreshadows a campaign of economy by the process of increasing the expenditures of the year previous. Now, if the government has not yet had this money voted and has spent it, and if there was no Governor General's warrant to authorize the expenditure, then it must have been against an account the moneys of which were voted for a totally different purpose.

The only explanation I
have had is the one I have given. If there is any other I shall get it and shall be glad to submit it to the committee.
A moment ago the minister referred to a loss by the department by reason of a loss in exchange. How could the department suffer any loss in exchange?

It was not a loss in
exchange. The difference in the amount inquired about is due to an increase in the exchange which had to be paid to the United States.

But surely that difference would be collected from the customer at the time of the purchase of the money order. I am quite aware that at one time you could not send five dollars to the United States without paying difference in exchange but one would have thought that this difference between the currency of the two countries would be charged the customer and that the government would suffer no lose.

There is a certain fluctuation in the total amounts, and the question was asked as to the reason for the difference between one year and another. The explanation that was given me I have already submitted to the committee.

What percentage of the
revenue goes to the local post office, and how much does the department receive?

I presume the question
refers to the money order business. In the revenue offices the percentages are, four cent? to the postmaster issuing the order and one cent to the postmaster paying it.

I understand that. I want
to know what percentage of the million and odd dollars goes to those who issue and pay the notes, and what percentage of this total goes to the department.

revenue derived pays the total expenses connected with it.
Yes, it does.

The minister has already explained the expenditure for two specific years which he compared, one of which carried a much larger number of postal orders than the other, and for the difference he gave two reasons:	First, the receipts of one year's
business were less than those of the other owing to a smaller number of orders having been issued; second, there was a loss of revenue owing to a difference in exchange. I

Supply-Post Office
dc not yet understand that question of exchange, because I cannot see how this country could sustain any loss whatever by reason of a difference in exchange. I want that thoroughly explained.
The difference in exchange, of course, had to be charged to the public.
Oh, that answers the question. Then there was no loss to the government on account of exchange?
No.
That is all charged to the public who buy the money orders?
Yes.
Then we are to understand that no portion of this loss of $500,000 is to be accounted for by any difference in exchange?
No.
What does account for the loss, then?
There is a difference between the two totals but there is no loss.
There is a distinct loss of some $500,000 and I understood the minister to say that no portion of that loss was to be accounted for by the question of exchange.
We do not call it a loss; I think my hon. friend has got hold of the wrong term.
There is a difference in the total returns to the department.
Yes, the total receipts in money order business.
That is to say, in commissions earned by the department; and no portion of the loss is accounted for by exchange. Is that correct?
Yes.
Where, then, does the exchange come in? It does not come in at all, and what I want to know is what accounts for the loss of $500,000 in commissions.
If the exchange were, say, two per cent, that amount would enter into the transaction and would go to make up the total.
But the purchaser would pay it, not the country, so that the question of exchange does not enter at all.
The purchaser has to pay both, but in settling accounts between the countries we have to pay out the difference in exchange to the United States.

But you have already received it. My point is -that the department's commission or profit is represented by the last figures given by the minister. If the purchaser of money orders pays this exchange, how can the country's revenue be affected by even one cent?

Do not the figures given by the minister a moment ago demonstrate the fact -that the country is ahead on exchange? In other words, according to the figures the customer is charged more money than the actual difference on the exchange; there -is a profit on -the exchange business besides.
My hon. friend is correct according to the situation as it exists.

Will the minister give the
House the reason f-or this decrease in revenue earned by the department from 1920-21 to
1923-24?
The only explanation is that the money is at par, and therefore now there is very little charged as against what was formerly charged.
Surely the money being at pax would not enter into the question of exchange at all.
Perhaps I should have said -almost at par.

Has not the department accurate, intelligible figures to give us some idea of the disposition of the $500,000? Other members may have been able to analyze the difficulty, but I certainly have not been able -to.
Will the minister give us again the total business for the two years under discussion?
The total receipts from the money order business in 1922-3 were $1,180,957.45; in 1923-4, $1,364,110.53.
Evidently the explanation is that in 1921-2, when the difference in exchange was greater, the government made a bigger profit on exchange than they are doing to-day when it is almost at par.

The explanation given me is that this year, when exchange is nearly at par, we are not collecting so high a rate.

You are not collecting so much money.

Agriculture-Dairying, including grant of $3,000 to the National Dairy Council, #?30,000.
What is the exact function of the National Dairy Council?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is an organization of dairymen extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It exists in addition to the provincial organizations. Its chief functions are: to keep track of the general dairy interests of Canada; to propose any new or any amended legislation that they think is required; and to see that the law is observed. Some members of this Council are now attending a series of conventions extending from Quebec right through to British Columbia. The work is of an educational charaoter. Formerly the vote was in the miscellaneous items. It cannot be paid out of the main vote without indicating the character of the grant.
We should have some explanation of how this money is expended.

Mr. Chairman, as my hon. friend, I think, knows, we have recently introduced a system of grading of dairy products, principally carried on in the city of Montreal, but elsewhere as wed wherever it is convenient to do so. This involves a certain amount of additional expense, but it has not necessitated any expansion of the grant, we having dropped some other work. Cow testing was discontinued last year, and handed over to the live stock branch. There is a considerable amount of educational and inspectional work going on all the time, but more particularly in connection with the grading of dairy products and infractions of the law. I am sorry to have to report that in certain centres there is a disposition to put on sale adulterated butter. It takes a good deal of care on the part of our officers and a considerable staff to check up this adulteration.
What is the butter adulterated with?

Oils-cocoanut oils, chiefly. We have only one report of an infraction of the law of that nature which got past the dairy graders. It is not always easy to detect the adulteration without an analysis. These are some of the activities of the dairy branch. The work of the combined 
creamery and cheese factory in the town of Finch, with which the hon. member (Mr. Kennedy, Glengarry) and others are familiar, is now completed. The work done there during the last twelve years has shown that a factory of fairly large proportions can be run much more economically and on a better basis than the small factory. I notice that the Ontario government is carrying out the same idea this year, that of encouraging the consolidation of small factories for the purpose of keeping down overhead and increasing the turn-over. This work having been completed we have sold the property at Finch and it has gone into private hands. We may later take up a similar demonstration for the province of Quebec.
Do we understand that this adulteration takes place in the creameries or butter factories? Or is it done by the dealers?
Very little of it is done in the creameries.
Where is it done?
It is done in the cities, where people make a business of buying butter and adulterating it.
By dealers?
I think we have only one case reported of its being done in the factory.
It is not done by individual fanners?
Oh, no. I am glad to say that the farmers' product is improving from year to year. It was very much needed for some of them.
Has the minister's department done anything in regard to setting up a uniform standard of grading of dairy products for the Dominion?

A uniform system of grading has been in force wherever grading is done provincially. It is only recently that grading has been done federally. The system of appointing butter graders is not yet quite uniform. In the three prairie provinces, where they started it first, we have adopted their grade certificates; that is to say, we have adopted their grades as federal grades in order to avoid overlapping. There is often some little mix-up in a system which is largely federal but which is provincial in some aspects; for example, sometimes by mistake these provincial certificates are issued, and follow the butter, instead of the federal cer-

Supply-Agriculture
tificates. The chances are that in time we will take over that grading in the three prairie provinces and make the system uniform. As to the scale of points and the score cards, these have been adopted by. the federal authorities in conjunction with the provinces and are practicably uniform.
Is the grant to the National Dairy Council an annual grant?
Y'es.
Is it the intention of the department at any time in the near future to adopt a system of grading of dairy products for home consumption as well as for export?

As soon as there
is any demand for it. We find that the public have about all the grading they care to stand now. You have to carry out these reforms more or less gradually. When it is remembered that we have adopted an entirely new system in the matter of the grading of cheese and butter for export, completely reversing the practice that had previously prevailed for thirty years, I think it will be agreed that we have done fairly well even in adopting a grading system for export alone. The home market has grown up as the result of a taste acquired by the public over a long series of years, and I do not think the people are demanding a system of grading of dairy products for home consumption. It would mean, of course, an increased number of inspectors and a greater cost. It will be a few years yet before the system of grading for export is fully accepted by the British importer, so we might wait a little while, before going further along the line -my hon. friend suggests. I understand that some of it is already graded voluntarily. The same .principle is adopted in regard to the inspection and grading of eggs; it is not a new principle. We have considered it inadvisable just at present to go beyond this voluntary grading.

I am disappointed at the remarks of the minister in. this connection. If I remember rightly, in the course of a conversation I bad with him last year he said that so far as the grading of idlairy products was concerned, Canada was twenty years behind the times-

Yes, that is right
-not quite twenty, perhaps.

-and if that is true his department should not hesitate to make up some of that time. His system of the grading of dairy products
for export has been working out admirably. But the neglect to grade dairy products for home consumption means that second-grade and third-grade cheese and butter are left for our Canadian consumers, and as our own people are not getting a first-class article they are not consuming as much of our butter and cheese as they should. Moreover, some of our cheese factories and creameries are working up a local trade, and in the absence of any system of grading they are making a low-grade product, or are at least failing to come up to the standard of the number one grade. One of our inspectors in Ontario recently showed me some figures with respect to last year's operations which demonstrated clearly that the factories catering to home consumption are not coming up to the requirements, are producing a high percentage of second grade cheese and butter For that reason I would urge upon the minister the desirability of requiring cheese and butter for home consumption to be graded as in the case of cheese and butter for export.

My hon. friend
has presented the case exactly as it is. It is a question, to some extent, of cost of operation, and also of the advisability of going ahead rapidly or otherwise. We have taken some pride in making progress. We started out late in the day in the matter of grading. If my hon. friend knew the number of kicks that have come into the department against the new regulations-not so much now against the dairying end of it, but at the beginning they were very numerous-he would be -more fully seized of the importance of going Slowly in the matter of these reforms.
Where are the kicks coming from?

I am free to admit, from the least important factor. However, I will be very pleased to take my hon. friend's suggestion into consideration, and if we can introduce about another three or four more graders we wTill probably do it, but every time we inflate the civil government list, there is always someone wanting to know, "What does all this mean?" So we have some hesitation in making the necessary explanation as to why this expansion. As a matter of fact, we have been starved all along the line, and if I had the freedom of expression I would like to have, I would tell my hon. friend that I would like to be able to meet him to-morrow, because after all we have adopted the very same principle he suggests in the matter of grading eggs. There is not much demand for it yet from the public. The objection has been on the part of the middle-
Supply-Agriculture

men,-the objection always is from them. They say we are interfering with their trade, that their trade is in danger to some extent. It is the old story that dates back to the early days of humanity-our trade is in danger. They do not like change.
How many graders are employed by the government in grading cheese, and what are their duties?

Their duties are to grade and inspect the cheese. The principal graders are stationed at Montreal, because that is the converging point in the export trade. There are two or three other places in the province of Ontario where grading is done. I have the names and salaries of the graders here. We have some twenty graders scattered throughout the Dominion, in addition to the ones we accept from the prairie provinces.
How many points are there in Ontario where this grading is being done?

Belleville and Toronto; there is also one in London part of the time. A great deal of the produce of Ontario, however, naturally gravitates to Montreal and is graded there, especially from the eastern part of Ontario. It would be very convenient if we had more places where grading could be done, but the more places you have the greater the expense.

Why is it that the government does not stand behind the grader's grading? I have in mind several cases where the graders have graded cheese as No. 1, and then it went over to the Old Country and was graded there as No. 2 or No. 3, and the buyer was billed back for it. And the government has so far refused to stand behind their own grader's grading; the buyer has had to bear the loss. I think this works out very unfairly to the buyer, and the government should certainly stand behind their own grader's grading.
Do we understand that in the eastern provinces there is no such grading of cream in the butter factories as we have in the west? Is the grading simply done on the manufactured product?

Anything that comes under the question largely of production is left to the provinces to take care of. We are trying to find a line of demarcation between provincial and federal activities, and speaking generally those activities that have to do with

production are left to the provinces, and matters respecting marketing and grading are left to the federal authorities. So the question of cream grading in the west has been a provincial matter, for some time. Hon. John Martin has introduced a bill in the Ontario legislature, however, for the compulsory grading of cream, for the first time in Ontario.
That is just what I wanted to know, whether they had a system of grading.

Replying to my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Thompson): It takes more than one or two years to build up a grading system that would be recognized by the British or any other market. They have been accustomed to private brands alone in the past, and may be buying on consignment. While we have adopted a grading system here, they have not become sufficiently familiarized with it yet to buy entirely on the basis of grade, but as soon as they get sufficient confidence in it and find that the grade is as indicated on the box, they will gradually accept our certificates at their face value. I do not know what my hon. friend means by saying that we do not stand behind the graders.

I say that cheese is sold here according to the government grader's grading. It will be graded No. 1 here, and sold as No. 1, and quite often the grade is changed when it gets to the Old Country to No. 2 or No. 3. The old country merchant refuses to pay for the cheese, and the government so far has refused to stand behind their own grader's grading.

I think I understand my hon. friend's point. It involves a pretty long story but I think I may take two or three minutes to try and explain the difficulty to him and other hon. members. Of later years the practice has been to ship cheese in a very green state. Just as soon as it has solidified enough on the shelf, and when it is still merely a bundle of curd, a great many factories are desirous of shipping it out. Obviously we cannot get a fair grading on cheese in that condition, and sometimes our graders absolutely refuse to grade it, because it is too green to get a grading that will do justice to the cheese and to the grader. In the Antipodes they do not have that difficulty because they have adopted the system of holding the cheese for a certain length of time before grading is permitted. In addition, after their cheese has been graded, there is a long voyage which permits further maturing before the cheese reaches the market. In the case of

Supply-Agricul ture
green cheese it is impossible to anticipate what bacteriological action will develop before it reaches its destination, and the graders have simply to do the best they can with that class of cheese. We expect to bring down legislation this session trimming up some of the shortcomings of our present Dairy Act, and the only thing I can suggest at the moment is that this question may possibly be dealt with by providing that the cheese must be, say, two weeks old before it can be removed from the shelves of the factory in which it is made. That would ensure a certain degree of development that would enable the grader to make a fair grading of what the cheese was likely to be at the end of its journey. The situation now is unsatisfactory, and the whole question is, how soon can we put that pressure on? I must make the statement now that a number of other improvements are necessary in the dairy industry in order to make our products more acceptable in the British markets. If my hon. friend thinks that to have cheese two weeks old before leaving the factory would be an improvement I agree that it would be a veiy substantial advance. We will probably make the change anyhow, but I do not think the period should be any longer than that. In order to know where they stand with regard to their returns from the farm people want to realize their profits. The urgency of their financial requirements necessitates their getting the returns from the sale of the cheese as quickly as possible.

Will the minister be good enough to give us an outline of the improvements that will be necessary in order to place our dairy products on an equal footing with the products of other countries in the British market?

It is not usual to anticipate possible legislation; that is usually talked over in council before it is brought down. I think I may say, however, that one of them will deal with the boxes. The cheese boxes, for example, certainly need to be of a better design. We have had photographs taken by our own officials in Great Britain of boxes of cheese on their arrival in that country. We have also had photographs taken bv disinterested friends, Canadians visiting England; and really the dilapidated condition of these boxes is enough to spoil the sale of the cheese, and would really have that effect were it not for the quality of the product itself. When these boxes of cheese arrive in such a topsyturvy condition it is most objectionable to possible purchasers and always hurts the sale
of the product. The same objection does not apply to butter boxes as to the present cheese boxes. I think the type of cheese box used in Canada will have to be remodelled; as a matter of fact the kind of wood employed in the manufacture, they tell us, is becoming exhausted in this country. So, in any event, we will be obliged to change the style of box. Every time the boxes of cheese are moved or handled they suffer deterioration. On arrival in Montreal when they are placed in the freight shed other breaks occur; in fact a break occurs every time the box is handled. With every process of handling the condition of the box becomes worse, notwithstanding the fact 'that it is wired; and the handling the boxes receive from the dockmen reduces them to a mass of wreckage by the time they reach the docks in Great Britain. I am not exaggerating in the least. As I say, I have seen photographs of cheese boxes as they arrived overseas and their condition was greatly to be deplored. I hope I shall have the support of hon. members-I know I shall be supported by my hon. friend from Viotoria City (Mr. Tolmie)-in endeavouring to effeet an improvement. The Australian and New Zealand box seems to me to be the ideal article; it is a six sided box, two cheese deep.
Then there is 'the question of the adulteration of butter with any kind of oils. In this connection I think something must be done besides merely prosecuting the offender. What does the prosecution amount to as a rule? The magistrate imposes a low fine; sometimes he lets his sympathies run away, with his judgment. In addition to instituting a prosecution I think we should have power to prohibit any factory found, in proceedings before the courts, to be guiLty of adulteration with various oils in the manufacture of butter, from exporting for a certain period of time. That course was adopted by the food board. I do not want to quote the food' board as an ideal example, but that was one plan to which that body had recourse and it proved effective. I think we might also, in the case of butter, prevent the exportation where adulteration has bean shown to have 'been practised.
Why the difference between butter for export and butter intended for home consumption?

There is a difference. No producer should be allowed to pursue a Course which would have the effect of destroying our foreign market. So far as home consumption is concerned we are assuming that
Supply-A gricul ture

the Canadian consumers will soon detect the fact, in the event of there being adulteration, and will manifest their resentment. The guilty parties also will be condemned by our own producers. If the practice were persisted in I think we might almost go to the length of closing the factory.
In other words, anything is good enough for the home consumer, but we must have a first-class article for export.
Everybody recognizes that the home market in Ontario, and some of the other old provinces is not very fastidious, otherwise we would not be so long in getting an improved product.

The home market for both butter and cheese is an important one and should be cultivated. If the Department of Agriculture does not take the dead very soon in seeing that the grade of butter and cheese for home consumption is improved, we shall be using before very long New Zealand butter-
Hear, hear.
-and Danish butter.

Just what will
happen.

I think that is a very important reason why we should lose no time in grading all butter and cheese consumed at home. I was somewhat alarmed by the statement of the minister of the recommendation he is going to make as to the time the cheese may be left on the shelves of the cheese factory. I think his object wouild be accomplished by refusing to grade cheese or butter under a certain age instead of requiring that the products be allowed to remain on the shelf for a fixed period of time.
It would involve a lot, of handling in Montreal.

That might be true but I would point out that some factories have no cold storage facilities, and to require them to keep cheese or butter on their shelves under those circumstances would involve hardship and difficulty.
The minister spoke about the factory at Finch, and its disposal to a private concern. I should like to know a little more about the disposition of that factory, and the compensation which was paid to the factories on each side of the Finch dairy station?

I may say that the patrons were first given the opportunity to buy this factory, and the conclusion was almost arrived at that they would do so. On second thought, however, the patrons concluded that it would be better for an outside company having a chain of creameries to acquire the factory if they would pay the desired price. It was thought it might be better for an outside body, a vigorous, thrifty institution that could do the very best for the patrons because of their financial abilities, to take over the property. It was sold for $25,000. We assume that that paid all the expenditure that was put into the factory, so that we got the educational value of the institution without any expense to the country. I am not familiar with the early histoiy of the factory, but I understand that some twelve years ago there was compensation paid, and the expenditure covered two factories. We have not got the detailed information. We find, however,, that the work of that consolidated factory, if I might call it so, expanded so rapidly that it enveloped two others more or less-one entirely and the other partially. One was owned by, I think, a Mr. Maclean. The amount of compensation in that case was arrived at by arbitration and was fixed at $3,000. The other amount, reached by a similar method, was $500. The principle of compensation was recognized at the beginning; I do not think we could go in and wipe out a man's investment without giving some compensation.
Did these men agree not to reopen their factories.
That was the agreement.

We have regulations on grading. Do they not cover the improvements which the minister has outlined. In the first place he is speaking of cheese which is too green. If I understand the regulations aright, it is the grader's duty to hold the cheese until they are properly cured and fit for market. If the boxes are not up to the standard the grader's duty at the present time and under the present regulations, is to put them in a lower grade.
What does the hon. member suggest? Would it be better to move them right up to Montreal, or wherever they are to be sent, and let them stay there in proper storage the required length of time?

Is that not what you have just outlined in the present regulations?

Supply-Agriculture

Yes, they have that authority and they exercise it, but it involves a lot of extra handling, and that means extra expense. I think it would be better for the factories to do what they are doing, and hold it in the factory. But then we would have one constant complaint from the factories that we are holding it too long. I am prepared to take into consideration any suggestions as to which is the better way. I think the custom in the Antipodes is to keep it in the factories of production. It is kept there, and each factory can store it in its own accommodation. If we adopted that system it would not involve such a lot of expense in re-handling at Montreal. I admit that in some of the local factories the place for storage is not of the very best. Frequently they have no control of the temperature; consequently that would be an additional argument why you should ship it to Montreal or some other place, keep it at the proper temperature, and grade it when it matured. It is a question of expense. The best way is not always the practical way because of the additional cost involved.

With regard to the question asked by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Thompson) a moment ago as to the government standing behind the grading of cheese, the question asked was as to cheese which had been graded as No. 1. The minister in his answer referred to cheese that was green and unfit for shipment going to the hands of the grader. The grader certainly would not grade it as No. 1. The hon. member for East Hastings asked1 about cheese which had been graded as
5 p.m. No. 1 by the grader here, and when it reached the Old Country was reduced to second or third grade. What about conditions of that kind where the loss falls on the shipper? That is the question the hon. member asks. The minister endeavoured to make it appear that the cheese was going there too green. If it was too green it would certainly be placed in the lower grade by the grader and not as No. 1.

No, it might have the elements of No. 1, but you cannot estimate what bacteriological action may develop on the voyage across. We have the same trouble with anything that is perishable. Butter is subject to change and is very difficult to grade arbitrarily in such a way that it will "stay put". Eggs and cheese are in the same category. The sooner you get butter and eggs on the market the more likely they are to hold their grading. With regard to cheese
the more it matures before being graded the
more likely it is to retain that grade. Of course, we have to take the chances of the grading in mixed shipments and having the article hold its grade. I think we have been shipping out too early and taking too many chances on the grade being held. Those are the conditions under which we feel we have something to learn yet in the matter of grading cheese, and even after we have learned it all, as long as it is graded in the neighbourhood of two or three weeks old, there will always be a liability of some of it going wrong. When butter is three weeks old and unpasteurized we have to grade it. In case it is pasteurized we have to regrade it if it is six weeks old.

Will eggs require
regrading?

You have to have
regrading to allow for deterioration.

I think the explanations given do not apply to conditions in East Hastings. The cheese are held there until they are properly matured for grading. The cheese board have regulations to that effect, and no cheese is allowed to be offered for sale until they are matured. In that section I have known cases where cheese properly matured, as I have stated before, have been graded as No. 1, and regraded in the Old Country, and billed back to the buyer. The buyer has paid on the cheese according to the government grader's grade, and it so suffers a great injustice. If this government appoints graders throughout to grade these cheese, in my opinion they should stand behind the grade given. If not the grading is practically a farce.

I do not think the hon. member understands the grading system at all; otherwise he would not talk in the way he has;-he will pardon me for my frankness. No government stands behind the grader s grade under the grading system of which he speaks. As far as humanly possible, it is graded according to the judgment of the grader. Who gave the buyer the authority to regrade our cheese? He is interested in grading it down. They can put it at what they like. We have to build up as near as possible a uniform grade according to our conceptions of what is proper, and the provinces aim at making that as near as possible what the consumer on the other side wants. Let me draw attention to the oldest system of grading that I know of in Canada; that is in respect to our grain. You can send a consign-
Supply-Agriculture

rnent of No. 1 or No. 2 northern ,to Great Britain, and it may be a little bit off the grade when it gets there, but there is no such thing as the government making good the discrepancy. That is not right. The idea is that, as near as humanly possible to make a grade by physical eye test, that is done, and if you keep it uniform and up to that, that is all the buyer on the other side expects. Every time, however,-and there is where the penalty comes in whether it be butter or wheat-every time a consignment goes over a little off in grade, that induces the buyer to bid less than he would otherwise because he knows he is getting an inferior article. The more we keep up to the standard the better and steadier will be the bid on the other side.

There seems to be a difference between the department and the shippers of cheese as to the interpretation _of the law. The hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Thompson) says you cannot ship cheese to the Old Country unless it is matured. The minister says you can ship it when it is two weeks old. Why endanger the cheese shipping industry by allowing shippers to ship before it is properly matured? The hon. gentleman says that is the law.
There is no law insisting on that.
There is no law insisting on the people holding cheese until it is properly cured?
No.

Then the department is
using very bad judgment, because you should not endanger the business of the country by allowing cheese not properly matured to go out.

We thought we were doing very well to get it started. We have inserted the thin end of the wedge, and got the principle of grading cheese fixed. We propose to tighten it up where it is weak. After thirty or forty years of grading western grain you will find, after the Grain Act comes down, there will be some amendments. If that be so in the case of a system that has been in vogue for over a quarter of a century, it is not to be wondered at if after two years we find it necessary to iron out some of the shortcomings in the present grading system. What we have at present is as stringent as the people will submit to at the outset. When the bill comes down I

think we shall be able to satisfy the hon. member as to the length of time the cheese should remain either on the shelf or in storage before it is graded.

So far as I know, there
is always a 'good market for Canadian cheese in Great Britain and I think the minister ought to bring down a law this session to compel the producers to hold their cheese until it is properly matured. There is no particular objection to having another law, for God knows we have had hundreds of laws enacted in this House since I have been here.

I was asked a
question as to certain changes and I referred to them. It is not usual to anticipate legislation.

When we are preparing for
the development of our dairy industry, particularly from the standpoint of our access to the foreign market, it is well that all our Standards should be raised at the earliest possible date so as to enable us to meet the keen competition of other countries. New Zealand by a strict grading system in butter, and in cheese particularly, shows signs of outstripping us in the British market, notwithstanding that we had a reputation of being the greatest cheese exporting country in the world two or three years ago. Since that time New Zealand has come into the market with a more uniformly reliable article and has been able to outstrip us in Great Britain. The minister at the earliest possible moment should take such steps as would enable us to compete with such countries as New Zealand, Australia, Denmark and other places supplying the British market to-day. We all know what excellent results have attended the grading of eggs, and if we adopted in the case of butter and cheese regulations similar to those that are in force in the grading of eggs I am- sure our position would be greatly improved and we should be able to compete with other countries with greater success. We should pay particular attention to the home market and supply that market with such goods as would keep out competition from the outside. We have conditions that are favourable to the production not only of dairy products but of all varieties of farm produce, and with such advantages as we possess we should be able at least to keep out of the home market the foreign competition which otherwise would work to our great disadvantage. This can be done if we go about it in the right way.

Are our exports of butter shipped in boxes bearing the grade marks?

Supply-Agriculture
Yes, and we rather encourage the idea of putting on a private mark or brand as well.
All our butter shipments dlo not go to the British market as Canadian butter; some have private brands?

Some exporters
like to retain the private brand, which they consider valuable on account of its association with the reputation they have built up. But they must have our brand in any case.

I want to impress upon the minister the necessity for a better grading system in the export of butter than we have had in the past. I understood the minister to say this afternoon that we would get a better grading system as soon as we asked for it. Perhaps I misunderstood him, but the matter was pressed in the House very strongly last session and the minister took a sympathetic attitude towards it; he gave us to understand that the people in the eastern provinces were 
not, however, prepared to submit to further regulations. This is a question on which we in the prairie provinces at least feel that we have a serious grievance. We have in those three provinces a cream grading system which prevents rancid or over-ripe cream from entering into the manufacture of butter at all. That means that we do produce a better grade of butter than is produced generally speaking in the eastern provinces. I was glad to hear this afternoon that Ontario is contemplating the same system. The point is this, that in the Old Country the butter from the prairie provinces, although it takes better than the product from the eastern provinces, is at a disadvantage inasmuch as the whole supply from this country is known commercially as Canadian butter. Naturally our butter is lowered to the general standard of all the other Canadian butter. A customer in England may buy a pound of Canadian butter to-day and find it perfectly good, but he goes back to-morrow and buys another pound of Canadian butter which is a little stale, and the consequence is that all Canadian butter is condemned. The customer, therefore, buys the New Zealand product which has been standardized to such an extent that one always knows what one gets. We should try to bring our system up to the exact standard of the New Zealand system. This is imperative if we are to compete with the New Zealand producer in the Old Country; otherwise we shall lose that market altogether. An examination of the figures shows that in 1922 we sold Great Britain 17,000,000 pounds of butter which dropped in 1923 to 4,000,000 pounds; 1 was glad to see that the figures had gone up a little during the past year, our sale having risen to 15,000,000. But we are not holding our own in the British market, which after all is the only market we have. In the face of the contracting market our production is expanding steadily, and if we examine the figures for the prairies provinces we shall find an enormous increase of butter in that part of the Dominion. In 1923 we produced 39,000,000 pounds and that has increased to 47,607,000 pounds in 1924. Going back over the table for the last six or eight years, we find the production steadily increasing and the prospects are that it will continue to increase in the future. So that in the face of a contracting market we are producing far more than we can consume at home.
I was rather surprised to hear the minister say this afternoon that we may face a serious slump in the butter market, and he spoke about the possibility of New Zealand and Australian butter being sold in Canada. Per-

In addition, we have certain other distinct advantages, more particularly in the prairie provinces. While the New Zealander is grazing his dairy cattle on land costing anywhere from $500 to $1,000 per acre, we have very
cheap land, and in a great many districts we can graze our cattle on wild land on which we do not even pay taxes. I for one am not prepared to admit that under equal marketing conditions New Zealand has any advantages over us at all; indeed, I believe that W'e have advantages over New Zealand. It is only a few shears ago that the government of that country was sending men to Canada to study our conditions and to find out how we were making butter; they even took men from here to teach them how we were producing butter. It seems to me we must wake up, we must take note of these conditions and proceed to meet them, or else be prepared to lose the British market.
The expansion of this industry is reflected in the prices. In 1922 the average price for creamery butter in Canada was 56 cents a pound; in 1923 it dropped to 35 cents; and in 1924-the figures are not available yet^-I understand they will work out at about 31 to 32 cents a pound. The possibilities are that next year there will be a still further drop in price. In fact when I left Saskatchewan about ten days ago butter was selling in country stores at 20 cents a pound, something hitherto unheard of ait. this time of the year. I would again impress on the minister the necessity of doing something to enable us to get a standardized article on the British market, an article that will be a guarantee to the British consumer that whether he wants a poor grade or a good grade he can depend upon getting it day in and day out at a uniform quality. It is not so much a case cf producing a better article as a standardized article, an article of such uniform quality that the consumer will know wfiat he may expect to get. There must be the fullest co-operation between all the elements that make up the dairying industry in

In the Manitoba Free Press of January 27, 1925, Dr. Grisd'ale, the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, is quoted as follows:

It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that if we are going to hold this market at all the situation must be dealt with immediately, because production is increasing to such an extent that people in the west are beginning to be discouraged, and if there is a still further slump in butter prices I know just what will happen. We have been doing a good deal to stimulate the dairy interest, we have been trying from one end of the country to the other to encourage our people to go into mixed farming, particularly in the prairie provinces. Hon. members all over the House have been pointing out to us repeatedly the necessity of mixed farming in the west. I want to remind them now that we are in mixed farming on the prairies to-day to a greater extent than are the farmers in the eastern provinces. A study of the trade figures will show that we are producing per farm more dairy products to-day than any of the other provinces. And yet you are continually telling us to go into mixed farming as a cure-all for our troubles. We want your assistance if we are going to continue this mixed farming, because with, the slump in the value of wheat and other grains we have had to fall back on the dairy industry; but with the prices dropping as they are to-day and our market contracting something must be done to maintain our position. The cream grading system in Ontario and the western provinces is helping to that extent, but if over-ripe or rancid cream is used in the manufacture of butter in the other provinces, it means that that butter manufactured from it will go with ours to the Old Country as Canadian butter, and will lower the general standard of the whole commodity. I should like to have some assurance from the minister that before this session is over he will do something to try and improve this grading system and put it on a uniform basis.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) misunderstood me when he said I promised a better grading system when the people demanded it. I did not intend to say that, and I do not think I did say it. The market reports show that a considerable quantity of butter is voluntarily graded in Canada even now. We grade at Montreal anything that presents itself for grading, whether it is for consumption in the home market or for export, but the grading is not compulsory with respect to home consumption as it is in the other. A certain amount of latitude must be allowed in connection with internal commercial transactions; it may not be desirable to hamper them with a grading system. You can even buy seed grain or oats from your neighbour without any requirement as to grading. It is only when you are selling to some one at a distance, to whom you cannot talk, that it is desirable to proceed on that basis. According to the market reports in the Montreal Gazette No. 1 butter is quoted at so much, No. 1 cheese at so much, and so on, which shows that the grading is recognized as applied to the product for home consumption. If we made it compulsory it might be' found very vexatious in the case of small transactions, which could not be carried out unless the grading requirement had been complied with. That is not the idea of a grading system.
I had particular reference to grading for export, not for home consumption.

I did not hear my hon. friend make any suggestion in the matter. We adopted that at the beginning as a basis, without any knowledge of dairying at all. Probably we did not know any better; we did not know any other way. For example, we have the Miners' Union in Nova Scotia and in Alberta; we have the Fishermen's Union on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts; we have the steel workers' unions; and each one of them is just as much 
entitled to a grant of $3,000 a year for the purpose of placing their propaganda before this country as is the dairy council.
