The minister has informed us that 25 fines were imposed for the mixing of foreign matter with butter. We were also led to believe that the creamery manufacturers in the country were not doing just as they should. The matter narrows itself down to this, that there is one creamery merely under suspicion without any conviction registered against it. It is possible that this creamery may have been a little careless, without having offended intentionally. But the fact is that in 25 instances foreign matter was mixed with butter, and in those cases there were convictions. Were these all individual cases, or were any of the 25 fines imposed on the same parties a second or third time?
Those 25 represent so many different parties I understand.

I have for a number of years back, even before the present government came into power, taken a strong stand against the adulteration of butter, and that was one of the reasons I objected to the manufacture of oleomargarine; I did not approve of the manner in which the manufacturers of this commodity were permitted to bring material into this country without a tariff and mix it with other stuff and offer it to the public for sale. And until we take steps to see that the Dairy Standards Act is applied to all parties and to all dairy products put on the market we shall have a good deal of this inferior stuff offered the public, to the ruin of our reputation for wholesome produce I am ready to admit that you will find a great deal of this in the province of Ontario. Dairy produce is one of the things the value of which as a foodstuff the people of Canada have absolutely overlooked notwithstanding the high cost of living. If a great deal more dairy produce were used instead of so much of these inferior articles people would be healthier and they would be better satisfied, and until we see to it that no adulteration takes place we shall not have a desirable state of affairs. With the army of officials which we have at the present time there is no excuse for this condition continuing. If 17

the minister, in the bill that is to be introduced, will see that a penalty is imposed which will be so drastic that no one will attempt anything of the kind, the effect I have no doubt will be salutary. But that does not preclude the possibility of this cheap article being imported into the country and placed on the market where no standard applies to such importations. There is no standard' in the case of this stuff that is brought into the country, although there is a standard of grading in the case of the butter we export. You can import an inferior article which is subject to no system of grading and do anything you like with it, but when it comes to exporting local produce you are confronted with a system of standardization. The people at home are therefore suffering as a result of the regulations; we are doing everything possible to protect the health of the people abroad while we are doing nothing to protect those at home.
The hon. member, I take it then, is in favour of extending the grading system to all products, both imported and exported, alike?

I am not very enthusiastic for a grading system. I have expressed myself with regard to this matter many times in this House, and I repeat now that I believe in competition wherever it is possible. I do not believe in too much nursing legislation; I do not think that we ought to do for people what they know a great deal more about than we do. This has been brought out by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Thompson) in regard to the cheese graded by Montreal as No. 1 and sent to the Old Country where it was sold as a lower grade. The minister asks, who has the authority over there to set aside our grading?
I did not say that.

I misunderstood
the minister then. The statement made by the hon. member was that cheese had been shipped in this way and the minister took exception to the purchaser over there designating the article a lower grade than that which had been fixed by his officials.

It is a matter of
judgment on both sides.

Well, there is one
thing certain, and that is that the purchaser knows what he wants and will pay according to the quality of the article. When you coddle people too much and do not allow their judgment full play you destroy it, just as the native faculties of a man atrophy
Supply-Agriculture

through disuse. I am not one of those who favour a good deal of the grading that is being done by the Department of Agriculture in another direction. Eggs for local consumption are graded in this country to-day, and eggs graded as No. 1 may be placed in a shop window where the sun can get at them through the glass and in twenty-four hours they are in such a state that they ought to be graded No. 3. People in that case have to exercise their own judgment, but the dealer might say that the eggs having been graded No. 1 he was not responsible for their condition. We have too many government officials in the country to-day. The minister is creating a whole army of unnecessary officials in connection with many branches of the Department of Agriculture and that this practice is having no good effect is borne out by the evidence which we have in the exports of produce of this kind-a falling off of 75 per cent in our butter exports last year compared with the year before. Is that a desirable state of affairs?
Our cheese shipments have increased.

I believe our cheese shipments have been higher in years gone by. The possibilities along this line are very great indeed. I know considerable dissatisfaction exists to-day because of the fact that cheese has to 'be shipped from the factory to some grading centre, where it is graded by people who do not come in contact with the manufacturer. If the grading was done at the factory, the manufacturer would know why his butter was not given first grade and would take immedate steps to remedy the defect. As it is to-day, he finds weeks afterwards, maybe months, that his product is graded as No. 2 or No. 3, he is at a loss to understand this lower grading, and very often blames the official, although it may not be his fault at all. The minister informed us this afternoon that grading for western Ontario was done at London.
Part of the time.
In the oldest cheesemaking district in the Dominion we find that grading takes place only part of the time. I believe the next grading station is at Belleville?
Toronto and Belleville.

Frequently it is
weeks, yes I guess many weeks sometimes, before the manufacturer of the cheese knows just exactly how it is graded.

A triplicate copy
of the certificate is sent immediately to the manufacturer and all other parties concerned.
Is the cheese graded immediately it is received or after it has been in the cold storage plant for some time?

If we adopted my
hon. friend's suggestion of grading cheese at its point of manufacture, we would have to employ three or four times as many graders at a corresponding expense, and the work would not be done as satisfactorily because it would lend itself to all kinds of switching of certificates once the grading goes out of the hands of the cold storage authorities.

Well, Mr. Chairman, it appears to me that wiith all our facilities for teaching people how to make cheese and butter those who are engaged in cheesemaking should be taught in the dairy schools how to manufacture an article of the quality most in demand.
That is a provincial matter.

Yes it is; and now
the government steps in and says, " No, we are not concerned about who makes the cheese, but we will see that it is graded, and if when the cheese reaches the Old Country it is found to be of a lower grade the dealer must lose the difference in price, and we are not prepared to stand behind our grade." Is that fair?

Do you know any
country where the system of grading is different?

I am speaking of
the practice here, and I am pointing out that it would be much more satisfactory and desirable to instruct our cheese manufacturers how to make a high-grade article. Let there be some competition along this line, and it will be unnecessary to have such an army of officials, whose activities are bound to have an irritating effect upon those engaged in the industry. If I were a manufacturer of cheese I would prefer the old practice under which the buyer attended our cheese markets and bought on grade, and if the cheese was a low grade the fact was pointed out to the man in the factory. To-day under the present system of grading the man in the factory may not know for some considerable time how his cheese has been graded, and naturally he is very much dissatisfied if he finds that it has

Supply-Agriculture
been given a lower grade than that which he considered its quality entitled it to receive. I am afraid no improvement has taken place under present methods.
Mr. WARlNER:	I think a great deal of
benefit should result from this discussion, but I should very much dislike to see the -item cut down. From my knowledge of the dairy business I am convinced that Canada depends a great deal upon its development, and I am glad that the government is active in promoting the industry. But I also feel that some of the criticism to-night has been timely. I would not oppose the grading of our butter for home consumption, but I have not studied this question so -much as I have the necessity of securing uniformity of grade for our export butter. Our home -market is good, but we cannot get -rich by selling to ourselves; we must export our surplus to bring money into the country. The prosperous condition of the dairy -industry in my part of the country has helped people to carry on, and many of them are doing quite well in the business. The hon. member for Mackenzie (MY Campbell) has dealt in detail with the subject of grading. As I pointed out last session, our disadvantage in respect of export trade as compared, for instance, with New Zealand, is that we have a limited federal jurisdiction and cannot encroach on the provincial field. I realize there is difficulty in securing export control by federal legislation, but if we could secure such control I am confident it would be better for us. My own province of Alberta has been improving grades until it has established a good reputation for its butter on the Old Country market. With respect to the 13,000 grant to the National Dairy Council, I do not stand for subsidies and bonuses more than other members of the House.
Ordinarily we are not supposed to ask for bonuses, but I know so well what the National Dairy Council have been doing that I think this $3,000 is well placed when it is put in their hands to help promote the dairy business in Canada. There seems to be some question as to how the National Dairy Council is formed. I know that in our province there are different sections of the dairy association: -the -producers' section have a representative an-d the manufacturers have theirs, the work, however, being that of one organization. I do not care to stir up the oleomargarine question, which has been referred to several times to-night, because I think it is dead; at any rate I hope it is. The National Dairy Council did much to bring about the defeat of oleomargarine in Canada; 17i
in fact, they were perhaps one of the chief factors in the fight. When we think of the work that the National Dairy Council has been doing for agriculture and for dairying we should not make mountains out of mole hills in regard to this vote of $3,000. It has 'been a great source of satisfaction to me that the present government have been as favourable as they have to the development of the dairy business. They may have made mistakes, but people who -do not make mistakes do not do much else. I have myseLf on several occasions suggested remedies for defects in the regulations or in the laws and I -believe we can improve them. If we try to help the government in -the improvement of laws and in the development of the dairy business we will get much further than if we simply find fault with everything they are doing. I am not trying to defend the government, because I think they are able to defend themselves; but we cannot afford to cripple the dairy business in order to get back a-t any political group or any political -party that is in power. We slhoulld deal with this matter on its merits; we should not allow prejudice of any kind to interfere with the building up of the dairy business. I am sorry -to hear that the export has fallen off; I am at a loss to know why. I am sorry also -to hear that so much butter has been imported. Some few years ago a dairy -concern that I was interested in was called upon to compete with the New Zealand butter on the Pacific coast. The New Zealand butter got established at that time among those who cared for a lightly salted butter and we had some trouble to get a butter that would Compete with it, mostly on account of its carrying so little salt rather than being of better quality otherwise. It was not that there was not enough or as good butter in Canada, but the butter th-at came from New Zealand was different from ours. However, I -think we have largely overcome that. Let us help the government to remedy the defects connected with the handling of our dairy products and their sale in th-e export market. Let us do the best we can and let us not depend on the government to -pass a law in -order to make us do good work and to produce clean, sweet-butter and cheese. We should not expect -the government to do it all; we -can do a whole lot ourselves.

For the information of
the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) I would like to read a clipping from the London Grocer dealing with the question of butter. It is as follows:
The present season-
Supply-Agriculture

This refers to the season of 1923.
-has witnessed an unusually heavy import of Canadian butter. In a general way the butter from the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta proved superior to the article produced in the eastern provinces, and commanded a higher price. This goes to show the value of united effort as exemplified by co-operation between the creameries and the provincial governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and these provinces have very efficient systems of government grading.
I understood the minister to say that the regulations for the export grading of butter were the same in New Zealand as in Canada; am I right in that?

Yes, as near as
possible.

Then I am inclined to
think they cannot be very well carried out. Judging from information I have had from private sources, from people who have been in the Old Country and have bought New Zealand as well as Canadian butter, and also from articles in the Old Country papers, I am convinced that our butter is not grading up to the standard. I do not refer to quality so much as to standard; it is not equal to that of New Zealand. This is a matter that should be thoroughly looked into. I have talked to a great many people during the last two years who have been in the Old Country and I am assured by them all that they cannot depend on the standard quality of Canadian butter being maintained. Would the minister give us some particulars with regard to the two sets of regulations, New Zealand and Canadian? The last information I had was that they were very different.

Even though the
standards may be identical, it does not follow that the butters are identical. New Zealand may score higher on the same standard than we do, and thus produce a most acceptable butter. It may be in the salting; it may be in the texture. They cater more to the Old Country market than we do. We depend almost entirely on the home market; we do not strive after the foreign market to the same extent that Australia and New Zealand do.

These essential qualities should, it seems to me, be provided for in the regulations-the salting, the flavour, and so on. Surely if the regulations are to be effective at all these things must be provided for. The question is a very important one. Nothing should be left undone to bring our butter up to the same standard as that of New Zealand.
fMr. Campbell.]

My hon. friend
does not see the distinction. We can put on paper what we like as a standard, but that does not make the butter; the quality depends upon the person who makes the butter. Australia and New Zealand seem to make butter that is more acceptable on the market to which we also send ours; they seem to comply with the standard requirements better than we do, and they get a better price. Here are the standards for grades of creamery butter in Canada. We have not the Australian Standard, but it is largely the same. I may say Dr. Ruddick was over in New Zealand and Australia a little over a year ago, and he got the very last word on dairy production there. About twenty years ago he assisted in laying the foundations of the dairy industry in New Zealand himself, and his work has been carried on there by another Canadian who succeeded him. The standards are as follows:

Scale of points for scoring butter
Points
Flavour	 45
Texture	 15
Incorporation of moisture	 10
Colour	 10
Salting	 10

Total	 100
Then it goes on to define what flavour means:
Flavour means fine, sweet, mild and clean. Texture firm, close, smooth and waxy.
And so on. If my hon. friend was abetter butter maker than I am, he would come nearer to that ideal. I am less competent, further away from that ideal than he is, but the standard is the same for us both. He merely succeeds in obtaining a higher score than I do. He may get 99 out of 100, and I may get 95, but we are both aiming at the same standard.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Should not the regulations be fixed so as to make it a different grade if a higher figure is reached? Suppose one scores higher than 45 in flavour for No. 1, should he not get some special grade? Surely there is some way of getting around that.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister if in his opinion it was the good quality of our butter which caused the United States to put a duty of 8 cents a pound against it, and if so, why is it necessary to spend this huge sum to further increase the quality of our butter.

Supply-Agriculture

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I think the action taken by the United States was simply in conformity with the general policy of their government. The farm bloc there have a little different idea of protection from the farm bloc in this House. They wanted to protect butter, so they put a duty of 8 cents against it. I do not think it was because of the special quality of our butter, but just on the general principle of keeping it out. I have another definition here of what the different grades call for.
Special grade butter must be made from properly pasteurized cream, showing no reaction by Storch test, total score 94 and over. Minimum score for flavour 41.
First grade of butter, total score 92, and under 94; minimum score for flavour, 39.
It goes on with the rest of the grades in the same way. The specifications for the different grades are set out just as are the specifications for the first three grades of wheat, for instance, with which my hon. friends are familiar. The statute fixes what shall constitute the first three grades of wheat, and the four commercial grades are determined by the Standards Board. These grades are applied in just the same way.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Is one individual capable
of inspecting cheese, butter and eggs, or have you three sets of officials for grading these three products?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I understand the
same graders will grade both butter and cheese, but not eggs. There is nothing to hinder them from grading eggs also, but it is not practical for the grader to take on too many duties.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Is anything being done
by the department to encourage our trade in butter with Germany? This year we shipped to Germany 862,000 pounds of butter; she is now our third best customer. I understand there are opportunities for a very large development of that trade there. I wonder if the department is doing anything to encourage it.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
That is a matter
for the Department of Trade and Commerce. We are exporting so little butter compared with our total production that we have no difficulty in finding a market for it in Great Britain, but as a matter of fact I did not know that any of our butter was going to Germany. I do not know that it. would hurt if more butter did go; I do not know what my hon. friend is referring to. Our butter will seek whatever market is the best.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: It will not always seek it if there is not some effort behind it upon the part of the department. What I am concerned about is the rate at which our butter production is expanding. The minister knows the history of the butter industry in western Canada. I am concerned as to the outlet. When we look at the figures here, we find that the United Kingdom is increasing her consumption of butter every year. This year there is an increase of 6,000,000 pounds over that of last year in her consumption, and last year showed a very considerable increase over the preceding year; in fact, I believe that for ten years the consumption of butter in the United Kingdom has been steadily increasing, and yet we do not seem to be holding our own in that market. It seems to me there is something wrong, and if these regulations of ours are the same as those of New England it must be that they are not as strictly enforced. There appears to be something lacking. I have been assured by people from the Old Country that our butter cannot be depended upon to be always up to the same level like New Zealand butter.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
For fear a wrong
impression has been left I want to repeat that a man who puts poor butter on the market may well be concerned as to the future price he will get, but the man with good goods need never fear that he will not get a good price for his product. There is always a bigger demand for high class dairy products than the supply.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Has butter which is imported into this country to be graded?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I understand that
is not compulsory, but it is inspected. I think my hon. friend is under the impression that poor butter is being imported and is used for diluting our better butter. We have no knowledge of that. The adulteration is invariably done with some of these oils, such as cocoanut oil.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The question I
asked w*as as to whether it was necessary to have this butter which is imported graded.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: No.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
It is not compulsory to have this imported butter graded, but it is compulsory if you are going to export butter to have it graded, regardless of what the demand may be abroad. With regard to ice cream, which has become quite an important branch of the dairy business on account of the dairy products entering into it,
Supply-Agriculture

the last report I have been able to get shows that for 1923 the value of the ice cream was $7,473,144, and that 89,809,600 pounds of milk went into its manufacture. If the minister is anxious to have an efficient and uniform system of grading let him turn his attention to the ice cream which is sold. A great deal of it is called ice cream, and I venture to say there is not a particle of cream in the mixture; that is well known.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I answered that
point earlier in the evening by saying that ice cream is under the Department of Health. Speaking from memory I think there is provision as to the amount of butter fat which it must contain, but the matter does not come under my department.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: It might, I presume, come under the Ontario Temperance Act. I can scarcely understand how the minister can contend that this should come under the Department of Health.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I	do not make
such a contention; the matter simply happens to be just there.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I think the minister, in view of the fact that 89,000,000 pounds of milk go into the manufacture of ice cream and that he is at the head of this particular branch of the department, ought to take steps to assume control of the matter.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I have troubles
enough without borrowing any more.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: There is no commodity to-day on the market which is such a deception on the public as ice cream, a great deal of water, powder and other ingredients being mixed together and frozen. The fact that it is frozen is perhaps one of the few safeguards about it. The large quantity of milk I have mentioned goes into its manufacture, but if some steps were taken to ensure the purity of ice cream the amount of milk might be doubled.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I agree with my
hon. friend entirely. I may say, however, that I think some grading was done last year by the Department of Health. There is no question but that there is a lot of spurious stuff called ice cream.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: The minister thinks the matter is under the Department of Health.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I said I thought it had been graded last year. I know it is under the Department of Health,

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
All I can say is
it is a most remarkable place to have it.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I agree with you.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) as to the desirability of grading cheese in the factory. Representing, as I do, a dairy section I may say that we have had grading for a great number of years. The grading was done in the factory and gave entire satisfaction. Let me point out further that the dairymen took the matter up and sent a petition to the Minister of Agriculture asking for the grading to be done in the factory. The Eastern Dairymen's Association met in the city of Belleville and there was an attendance of some three or four hundred delegates. A vote on grading in the factory was taken, and there was a unanimous expression of opinion in its favour. The minister was represented there by Mr. Duncan Marshall, and he informed the dairymen that he would convey their views to the minister. A deputation was also appointed which went down to Ottawa and urged upon the minister that grading be done in the factory. The minister says it is impracticable to do this but in view of my extended experience I disagree with him. I know that a grader can grade three counties. The grading is practically done in the first two days of the week, and the grader has virtually the rest of the week to himself, so there is nothing to hinder him from driving around and inspecting the product of the factories. There would be an educational feature about doing it that way. The grader could explain where the defects in the cheese lay, and those defects could be more quickly remedied. At the present time the cheese are sent to Montreal, and the minister says a certificate comes right back. Well, it takes a few days for the cheese to arrive there and a week elapses, sometimes two weeks, before the certificates come back. I know this for a fact. I see a great many certificates and I know what I am talking about. In the meantime the maker has made perhaps a few thousand dollars worth of inferior cheese before the certificates have been returned. If the cheese were graded in the factory and defects were discovered an inspector could get there and recommend remedial measures at once. The minister asked the hon. member for South Oxford what other countries guarantee the grading. I want to say that no other country, to my knowledge, ships in just the same way that Canada does.	It is true that
grading is in force in New Zealand, but regrading is done and the purchaser does not

Supply-Agriculture
have to bear the loss. The minister has referred to the conditions in New Zealand being superior to ours. With that I do not agree; I believe we have the best known system in the whole world to-day. The cheese are bought in Canada, and the farmer gets his money the very day of the sale. At any rate this is the system in central Ontario; I cannot speak with so much certainty as to the practice farther east. Cheese from New Zealand is consigned to firms in the Old Country and is dumped on the market. Quite often a lot of New Zealand cheese is dumped on the market at once, with detrimental results to Canadian cheese, and a reduction in price.
I reiterate my request that some explanation should be given with respect to the vote of $3,000 for the National Dairy Council. The minister has not yet given one word of explanation as to what is to be done with this money. Outside of this particular vote, thousands of dollars have been spent in entertainment and the payment of expenses, but no details have been vouchsafed as to what the council did last year.

speechtext:
Shall the resolution

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Last year we paid the travelling expenses of the delegates of this association, and several hundreds of dollars additional were incurred in entertaining
them when they arrived here. I do not believe the minister gave us more than one-half of the names of the members of this association.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
That is right. I
thought it would be tiresome. I have them all here.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Would the minister inform the House who appoints the members of the National Dairy Council, and how they are appointed?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
By the various
dairy bodies throughout Canada, about twenty. The associations are as follows:
The British Columbia Dairymen's Association, The Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association, The Alberta Dairymen's Association, The Saskatchewan Dairymen's Association, The Western Canada Ice Cream Manufacturers' Association, The Manitoba Dairymen's Association, The Eastern Ontario Dairymen's Association, The Ontario Milk and Cream Produce Association, The Canadian Creamery Association, The Canadian Ice Cream Manufacturers' Association The Milk Producers' Interests, The Condensed Milk Interests, The Canadian Milk Distributor's Association, The Quebec Dairymen's Association, The Montreal Milk Producers Association, The New Brunswick Dairymen United, The Dairymen's Association of Nova Scotia, The Prince Edward Island Dairymen's Association, The Holstein Friesian Association of Canada, The Canadian Ayreshire Breeding Association, The Canadian Jersey Cattle Club.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: In view of the large grant which the Canadian National Dairy Council receives, does the minister approve of the action of its secretary in taking an active part in electioneering work while holding office?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I was not aware
that he did so. I suppose he has a right to exercise his franchise, even if he is a member of the association. We have nothing to do with appointing him or paying him. I do not control him in any way. Here are about twenty organizations without political predilections that I know of. They appoint Mr. Scott as their secretary. I do not know what we have to do with his political 10 p.m. activities, admitting that he does exercise these activities. I do not know that he does. He is responsible to these organizations who have appointed him and pay him, and if he has gone wrong they can call him to account.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Is there any renovated
butter being manufactured in Canada?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Not that I know of.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
What becomes of the rancid butter that is unfit to eat.
Suppl y-Agricult ure

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I think it is shipped to the Old Country and the United States.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: For renovating purposes?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: It is more a blending process, melting it down. In the United States I think it is renovated as well.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: And what is the average yield of the dairy cow in Canada.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: About four thousand pounds.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: What improvement have they made in the last three or four years?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: It is very hard to tell. I think it is by a generous computation that we credit them with four thousand pounds. I had an estimate of the general increase and I think it was about 10 per cent. I question very much whether it is over four thousand yet. As a matter of fact a great deal of it must have been below four thousand to make the average an even four thousand. It is improving a little bit.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Is cow testing still being carried on?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Yes, under the Live Stock Act.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: In view of the great importance of increasing the average yield of the cows of the country, with a view to cheapening the cost of production of dairy products, what steps is the department taking at the present time to improve the quality of our cattle?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I think that is really provincial work. In some of the provinces they have been engaged at it for some years, -Saskatchewan, for instance. Where the other provinces will not take it up we deal with it. Apparently some of the provinces are not alive to the importance of it. My hon. friend has struck the weak spot in our dairy industry-the low product per cow. It is astonishing how many boarders are kept in our herds. The matter should be taken up by the provinces. Some of the provinces, to their credit, have taken it up, and others are gradually taking it up and where they do not take it up we handle it.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Would the minister be consistent, fix the standard of production for the cow and appoint inspectors to go round and see that the standard is lived up to? The minister has pointed out that these dairymen's associations appoint the members of the dairy council. The minister knows very

well that the dairymen's associations are not really dairymen. They are the dealers who are engaged in purchasing and handling dairy products. As far as Ontario is concerned I think that is the case.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I think the hon.
member is wrong.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
In the dairymen's
associations I think you will find the majority are engaged in that business, and they are anxious that this grading should take place, just as the packing house people are anxious that the department should undertake the grading of their hogs. This is well known. There is no more excuse for the government stepping in and grading the hogs that are sold on the market than there is for grading anything else. The packing houses should purchase the hogs according to the grade, just as they do beef animals, and it is just as reasonable to fix a standard for beef animals and compel them to be graded as it is to grade hogs. The packers could do this work, and they have no one to blame but themselves if the standard of pork in this country is not as high as it should be. They could pay the price the hog was worth, just the same as they could in the case of a beef animal, and yet the department are not grading these animals. They are not grading the butter which comes into this country, but they are grading the eggs that are laid, and there is no possibility of adulterating an egg. It is in a case which defies anyone to put any mixture into it. It is simply a matter of sizes and quality. It is one of the simplest questions that could possibly be dealt with, and I question if those who are purchasing eggs for use in their homes know a small egg when they see it. If the minister wanted to do something that would satisfy the full demands of the public, he would compel people to sell eggs according to their weight. But to appoint an army of graders and put them loose on the country and disturb conditions by the threatening attitude they are assuming to-day will do much to discredit the egg business in the country, and if it continues I question whether the government will not be forced to drop the system which they have adopted. They have people going round through the country at this time threatening that if the eggs are not sold according to grade the producers are going to be prosecuted immediately. They are not going to tolerate it any longer. What is the result to-day? No. 1 eggs of the highest standard are being sold as No. 2, because in this way they can avoid the penalty, and consequently eggs that should sell for a higher

Supply-Agriculture
price are being sold at a lower price. The consumer has to go and purchase the grade of eggs, and as a result is paying more than he should for those eggs. It is an unnecessarily aggravating restriction that I believe is going to do much to create dissatisfaction in this country. And this army of officials who have been turned loose on the country are the biggest menace we have.. The people of the country are intelligent, and we have schools to educate them to do things as they should be done. But when it comes to the National Dairy Council, I believe that a more useless body does not exist in the country, notwithstanding what others may say to the contrary. I believe I know what I am talking about when I make that statement. Now, it is only a short time ago since the minister altered the standard with regard to hog grading, raising the maximum weight by 10 pounds; and after the people had been compelled to accept a lower price during all that time it had been in effect the admission is made that it was all wrong. So that the people have had to suffer a loss at the hands of the department without being reimbursed. For the 10 pounds per hog they were forced to take a lower price. I put a question on the order paper last session to ascertain whether the department would reimburse them; for undoubtedly they have suffered at the hands of the department. The department admits that it was wrong so that the whole thing was merely an experiment, and now the minister is out with his egg-graders and is experimenting along this line. I am sure that this new experiment will work to the injury of both producer and consumer, because after eggs have passed through all these different processes of grading, entailing an additional expense, they will cost the consumer so much that he will be inclined to do with less of them. And if the producer is forced to sell his eggs as seconds to avoid anything of this kind he certainly will not receive as much as he formerly got for his produce.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I would point out
that we are discussing the dairy vote and I am afraid the hon. gentleman is off his eggs.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I was making a
comparison between the different systems which the minister is developing and which are all along the same line. There is a National Dairy Council, and that was the matter that wias under discussion; and the minister apparently does not know where the money is going. In view of the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Thompson) that Mr. Scott, the secretary of the association, and the present organizer of the Liberal party, had both been
in his constituency talking to the people there, and had both been getting their money out of the Department of Agriculture, voted by the people, I think the hon. member is justified in suspecting that some of the money will find its way into the pockets of some of those who have been stumping for the government. We have been deceived in this respect before and it is quite possible that the same thing can happen again. I remember one night questioning an item in the minister's estimates and it was allowed to go through without an explanation, the committee being misled. Afterwards the minister absolutely refused to go back to it; he thought it was very clever to have got the item through that way and he laughed about it. A similar item has not appeared in the estimates since.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. member is referring to.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I made it clear; I
mentioned two names of men whom I had been discussing. One is now under discussion, the other having been discussed on that occasion.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I was wondering if the minister would not concentrate on the Old Country market for butter. The British people are the greatest consumers of our exportable surplus of some 15,500,000 pounds. The minister might be living in Liverpool or in London and might secure to-day five pounds of Canadian butter bearing the Canadian brand with all the necessary qualifications. He would find this butter perfectly satisfactory, and going back to-morrow he would be unable to get more of it, simply because we could not export enough. The 15,000,000 pounds which we export to Great Britain will provide one-third of a pound per capita for the people of the Old Country, so that we are making a big noise about .nothing. My contention is that we should concentrate on the British market which will prove of considerable importance to us as our exports increase. We are doing good business on the British market and I do not think we should make any special effort to invade other countries. When my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) was speaking of eggs he said that this article went through so many processes that the price was increased so that the purchaser was bound to use less and less of it. I would remind him of the fact that they will use still less owing to the tariff. When we seek to enter the German market or any other market for that matter where they compete successfully with us, the moment we produce an extra No. 1 quality the people of that particular country will treat us in the same way as the United States have
Supply-Agriculture

treated us, by putting on a tariff against us. What benefit, therefore, shall we derive from developing that market? I argue for concentration on the British market; we get in free of duty, and our activities should be confined to that field.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Is the Finch cheese and creamery factory run as a commercial proposition or for experimental purposes?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
It was started as
a demonstration about twelve years ago to prove that a large factory with a large turnover could produce butter and cheese more cheaply than could a small factory. One would not think that this would require any demonstration but apparently it does, because 90 per cent of the factories are too small to afford the payment of good manufacturers. You do not, therefore, get- the best results under such conditions. Having demonstrated that fact by statistics and results we feel that the work has been completed and have sold the building. We hope to take up similar work in Quebec later on.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
What were the results of
the demonstration, in dollars and cents.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The patrons themselves would be better able to answer that question; the fact that we could not take care of the large numbers who wanted to take advantage of the facilities is sufficient proof of the success of the undertaking. The patrons of that dairy station were charged regular rates for manufacture. They received in premiums over and above the average price, as much as $18,000 in a year; and during the period of government operation they received over $100,000 in premiums just because the factory was equipped to make butter and cheese and sell milk or cream to the best market. A good deal of the product was sent either to Montreal or to the American market, according to where the greater advantage lay. The factory was able to show satisfactory results inasmuch as there was a large turnover. The supply of milk increased from 2,069,000 pounds in 1912, the first year of operation, to 11,500,000 pounds in 1924. This, I think, will show the popularity of the institution as well as demonstrate the fact that a large turnover makes for the reduction of overhead per pound. The revenue received from the Finch dairy station, together with the sale price, exceeds the total expenditure on the establishment. Thus the dairy branch has had the advantage of practical experience in operating a large factory at no cost to the government whatever, and the farmers in the locality have received over $100,000 more than

they would have received had they continued to operate the two small factories which were combined to make the Finch dairy station. I think this work was started under one of my predecessors, the Hon. Martin Burrell, and I wish to compliment him on the outcome of the demonstration.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Why did not the minister
continue the good work if it was so profitable?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Because the demonstration has been completed. The present government of Ontario has taken the cue to some extent from the successful operation of that factory, and is bringing in legislation to consolidate the small factories and encourage the construction of larger factories. So I think our work was justified.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Who bought that factory?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: The business in the district is becoming almost entirely confined to the cream trade; therefore it 'is difficult to carry on work in connection with butter and cheese. The station had become so large and cumbersome, and the demonstration had been so successful that we could not make it more so. The patrons to-day are shipping their cream in large quantities to both the United States and the Montreal market, and the business to-day is a purely commercial proposition.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Are the patrons deprived
of the advantages which the government provided at the dairy station?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The patrons were
in favour of selling the factory, and we gave them the first opportunity to buy it.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Who bought it?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: The Canadian Milk Products Company, at $25,000. We got back all our expenditure-made the experiment for nothing.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
What capital investment
did the government make?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
About $20,000.
Additions were made to the station from time to time as the business grew.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Was $20,000 the original
capital ?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: No, it cost originally about $15,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Does this vote include any money expended upon the Finch dairy station?

Supply-Agriculture

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Then the discussion is
not in order.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my inquiry a short time ago with regard to the butter fat yield of cows in Canada was prompted by a question I asked a very prominent creamery man in a certain province during last summer.
I was astounded to learn from him that the average yield of the cows supplying his creamery was only 90 pounds of butter fat during the year, indicating that he could hardly be carrying on dairying at a profit, and the absolute necessity of adopting such methods as would improve the quality of his cattle at the earliest possible date. Is the minister still continuing the policy of distributing pure bred dairy sires?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Yes, we are.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Is the minister doing anything in connection with advance registration work of pure bred dairy sires?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Yes, we are working in co-operation with the provincial organizations. We had a conference at which we discussed the question of advance registration of breeding animals. I forget what stage it has reached, but I know the proposal was very popular among the breeders, and it was taken to be an absolute requisite that if a buyer was to get value for his money he must know the production of the animal and its strain. I understand that the different breed associations are now engaged in discussing the teTms under which animals will be admitted to advance registration.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
You have not got the
standard settled yet?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I think not.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
What was the item
last year in the estimates for the Finch dairy station, and is there an increased appropriation this year?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
No vote has ever
appeared in the estimates for the Finch factory. It was simply a subheading under the general vote.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I have before me the
Auditor General's report in which there is an item for the Finch creamery of $15,096.06, with the details specified, then an item for refrigeration of cars, followed by the general item, making a total of $226,000. Compared with the estimates for this year the figures in the report are lower.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I think the hon.
gentleman means that last year we had the cost of administering the Finch factory; this year we have not.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Then the estimates should be that much lower this year, but they are not.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
We hope for a
little expansion in certain other activities. If we have the money we will probably start a similar institution somewhere in the province of Quebec, giving the same demonstration in that old province as we did in Ontario.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I would suggest to the
minister in all seriousness that there should be no further expansion of capital expenditure except where it is absolutely imperative. The country is burdened with taxation that' is invidious in comparison with the taxation of other countries and is faced with railway deficits. Surely the minister and his colleagues understand the temper of the people. I should hardly think that in contemplation of an electoral campaign, which certain events seem to point to, the government would expect to receive popular approval of any expansion of capital expenditure. As a matter of fact the estimates do not disclose any serious effort on the part of the government to practise that rigid economy which the public and many hon. members believe should be practised in these very serious times, and I am surprised that the minister should speak of expansion of capital expenditure in such casual terms without offering any explanation.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I will speak when
my hon. friend is through. We cannot both be standing up at the same time.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
We do not seem to be,
either.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
No, and I do not
intend that we shall be.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The minister has plenty
of chances to stand up. The trouble is that he does not speak to the point, but around it. I do not think we have had the information to which we are entitled. I have referred to the Auditor General's report and the decided increase involved in the estimates of this year. The minister says that is expansion, but what it covers the committee is at a loss to understand.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Now that my hon. friend has sat down I will stand up. Yes, it is quite explainable. If I understand my hon. friend aright, he thinks we should stand still and not expand.
Supply-A gricul ture

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: No:

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
Is that the idea,
that we should not expand in any particular?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I think -expenditures should be cut down.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
In dairying? I
had not heard that note struck; on the contrary, I have had complaints from practical dairymen opposite me that we should extend our activities. I would like to meet all hands, but when two views are diametrically opposed I cannot meet both.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I do not want the minister to misrepresent my statement.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: It has always been the intention of -the department that when the Finch demonstration was over we would transfer those activities to another province and give them- the same advantage. Possibly when we are through with Quebec we may, if necessary, go on to the Maritime provinces. This kind of thing is needed very badly, especially in the two older provinces where there are such a large number of small creameries and factories. As to the Finch factory, I have shown that we got back our $25,000 plus 1100,000 to the patrons over and above what they would have got if we had not carried on this experiment. That looks to me like good business, and we might well continue the work.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I wish to correct the minister when he throws out the inference that I suggested any standstill policy. The minister speaks of expansion, but he does not tell us what that expansion is to consist of.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: I have done that.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I have not heard it yet,
and I do not think other hon. members have. This discussion originated out of the minister's statement that a little margin was being provided for expansion, but we do not know what the expansion is to consist of.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I must be a very
poor explainer. I said we hoped to establish a similar demonstration in the province of Quebec now that the work had been completed at Finch.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Is provision made for that in these estimates?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: What is the plan the minister has in mind?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
To repeat in
another province the experiment we carried out in Finch.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Is the place selected?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: No.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
What plans have been
formulated?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
We shall be able
to proceed on the basis of our experience at Finch. We have not yet determined where the factory will be located. I suppose we will have to follow the precedent established in Ontario by starting where three or four factories already exist, and dispose of them in some way. There is no use in starting on that until we know whether we get the vote through.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The province is selected,
the nature of the factory is determined. What further plans has the government formulated?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The same as at
Finch, except that we will build the factory all at once, not in pieces as we had to do before we knew what size would work to the best advantage.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The	minister has
now given out information, after a long series of questions, that he might well have given at the outset.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I	have given it
three or four times already.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The	minister has
not given it three or four times, unless within the last five minutes, so far as the transfer of the creamery at Finch is concerned. I think I have followed the proceedings tonight pretty closely, and until the hon. member (Mr. Ladner) brought the matter up I was under the impression from the statement made by the minister a little while ago that this amount was being dropped out of the estimates. Now we are informed that it is the intention to open up the plant in another place. A few minutes ago I asked with regard to the cow testing and was informed that that came under the live stock branch. Last year some $24,500 was expended for this purpose, under the item we are now passing for dairying. The minister informs the committee now that this passes into another item of the estimates. Here is a reduction of nearly $25,000 for cow testing, and another, I do not know how much, in connection with the Finch creamery, which indicates that there has been an increase of between $30,000 and $40,000 in the estimates under this head for this year. The committee would like to know what this increase is for. The items are entirely different from what they were last year if $25,000

Supply-Agriculture
for cow testing is taken out and the amount for the Finch creamery is also taken out. Does the minister propose to make up this increase in government officials? Nearly one-third of the amount last year was for that purpose. If he will tell us what the increase is for he will save a lot of unnecessary discussion.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: My hon. friend heard the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) and two or three others raise a point as to the advisability of making our grading system uniform. I explained that we had partly adopted the provincial system and that we hoped to make that uniform. Then we have the Bacteriological office, and the new station we contemplate establishing in the province of Quebec. That is what we have iD view.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
What will be the
estimated cost of these three activities?

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: Seventy-five thousand dollars is about what it costs for the grading now. The factory similar to that at Finch will cost in the neighbourhood of $25,000 if the same kind of building is put up. Possibly by putting it up all at one time we will save enough to offset the increased cost ol construction compared with that of twelve years ago. The cost of the Bacteriological office will be about $5,000.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The minister evidently is going to withdraw the last of the experimental farm stations from the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario in the past has been carrying on practically all of this work with the exception of the central farm here at Ottawa, which is for the whole Dominion, while the province of Quebec is simply dotted with experimental farm stations and demonstration farms, and now they are going to receive another one, for $25,000 of this item is to establish a school in the province of Quebec. I think it would only have been fair that the minister should have advised the committee of this when he introduced his estimates. He proposes to take this station out of the province of Ontario and put it over in the province of Quebec, where they have already lots of them, and which province is receiving ten times the amount, yes more than that, for experimental work that the province of Ontario has been receiving. The province of Ontario has been doing this work itself and paying for it out of its own provincial estimates, while the other provinces have been coming to the federal government and getting them to carry
on this work for them. Now we learn that the province of Ontario is to be punished for something, and that somebody else is going to be rewarded for something, because I cannot see any other justification for it than that. The minister has not explained why this is being done.
With regard to cow testing, there was an item of $25,000 in the Auditor General's report last year which was paid out of this vote. The minister now quietly informs the committee that this is going to be placed under the Live Stock branch and will not come out [DOT]of this item at all. Consequently there is $25,000 there. We are also given to understand that this item is to pay for a whole lot more graders than we have had in the past- govtemment officials by the score, costing hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the minister says, "Oh, we have not got a chance to expand. Vote us more money, and we will appoint another army of officials, and that will make farming prosperous."
The minister admits to-night that the exports of butter from this country to the Old Land last year decreased by 75 per cent over the year before. Surely this is enough to condemn the system which is in evidence everywhere in this country at the present time. I would like to ask the minister what amount will be required for the payment of these additional graders to whom he has referred.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: It just depends on whether we take the views of the hon. member for Glengarry and go ahead and grade all the butter, or whether we take the views of the hon. member for South Oxford and just chew the fat. It will cost about $15,000 altogether.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
The minister has a very clear idea as to what he intends to do when he comes before this House with his estimates. It all depends upon what the hon. member for so-and-so or somebody else thinks about it. He will take the views of this member and that, and strike a happy medium finally, but at the present time he is in the woods. He does not know where he is, or where he is going to land. This is a new way of bringing estimates before the House. I think the minister is almost unique in that respect, and if we are going to have all the estimates dealt with in this way, we are going to have a considerable lot of time taken up dealing with them. The minister is going to find out before he spends this money what are the views of so-and-so. Evidently he understands what are the views of the
Supply-Agriculture

people of the province of Quebec with regard to the creamery which is now situated at Finch in Ontario. He thinks they are more entitled to it than the people of Ontario. Would the minister tell us whose views he is agreeing with when he does that? Is he agreeing with some hon. member of this House who has expressed the view that that should be done?
The minister knows perfectly well that the federal government are conducting practically all the experimental farm work in the province of Quebec; they have half a dozen experimental farms there, and a dozen, demonstration farms maintained by the federal government, and I do not think there is a single one in the province of Ontario, with the exception of the one on the Transcontinental at Kapuskasing, and a small tobacco farm of forty acres at Harrow. That is the extent of the experimental work this government is doing in the province of Ontario. In spite of all the apparent discrimination against this province in the past, matters are now going to be worse because the station at Finch is to be transferred to the province of Quebec. The minister says that if he agrees with the hon. member for so-and-so he is going to spend some of this money for graders of some kind, and all the committee is supposed to do is vote this sum blindly, and let the minister do with it just as he pleases. That is practically the policy the minister is adopting on this the first item in his estimates. Why does not the minister frankly and straightforwardly inform the committee what he proposes to do with this money instead of our having to drag the information out of him as we have had to do to-night? At this late stage of the debate on this one item we are now informed what he intends to do with a part of it, but as to the other part he has not yet decided. All we are expected to do is to vote the money, and if he agrees with the hon. member from some place or other he will do so-and-so, and if not he will do something else. Surely that is no system upon which to base a request for this committee to pass an estimate. The minister should know what he proposes doing with this money if we vote it. It is not his money; it is not ours; it is the money of the people of this country; they will be taxed for it and have to pay it out of their pockets, and they are entitled to know what is going to be done with it.

I would like to know what is the cost of transporting butter from Calgary by way of the Panama canal to Liverpool, and by way of Montreal to Liverpool;

also the cost from New Zealand to Liverpool, and the cost from the Argentine Republic to Liverpool.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
I have not the
figures here. Some of the western butter goes by way of the Panama canal, and some by way of Montreal. It just depends on what kind of despatch they can get. Shippers by way of the Panama canal have had some difficulty owing to the butter contracting a fruity taste as a result of shipping it with oranges. I do not know whether that is going to deter the butter from going that way at all. A lot of shippers in Alberta I think prefer shipping by way of the Panama canal. That route attracts butter as far east as Regina sometimes. I do not think there is much difference in the rates. It depends on how long they can afford to wait. If the market is rising they do not like to ship by way of the Panama canal, and if they want to get to the market before it drops the butter will go by Montreal, because that route is quicker. We have not got the different freight rates here, but there is not very much difference.

The appointment of officials apparently is his idea of expansion. If the minister would undertake to present a detailed statement before the committee as to what amount was intended for each branch of the department under the head of dairying it would facilitate matters very much, and I would suggest that the committee rise and that the minister present us with a report of that nature when the matter comes before the House again.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext: The applicants for this bonus receive it when they comply with the conditions under which it is given. maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER

Cold Storage Warehouses, $30,00C.

maintopic: STANDARDS I OR GRADES OF CREAMERY BUTTER
speechtext:
This is a small item for the cold storage facilities of this country. The organized farmers of Ontario at least are developing a co-operative market and a pooling system, and in order to carry out the enterprise successfully it is necessary to have adequate cold storage facilities. There are certain seasons of the year when there is over-production in butter and eggs and so forth, including fruit as well, and there are other seasons when there is a light production, not enough to satisfy the demand. At these times there is a scarcity, with the result that prices increase. In overcoming the difficulty cold storage facilities would prove of considerable advantage, and it would help to some extent to relieve the situation to which the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has referred, namely, the importation of eggs and butter of an inferior quality at

Supply-Agriculture

certain periods of the year. If we had suitable cold storage facilities to take care of our products and enable us to put them on the market as the demand occurred it would help the situation remarkably, and would level up not only prices during the whole year round, but the quality of the produce as well; that is to say, there would be a uniform quality. I believe it would be wise for the minister to go into the cold storage question more fully. While we are anxious to cut down expenses so far as we possibly can, there are many other items which in my opinion might better stand a reduction, with more beneficial results. But certainly we should encourage the establishment of cold storage facilities in the country.

speechtext: I think there was a great deal of exaggeration, and a great deal of wrong was done to those services by the charge he has referred to.
